provenance.label: School Project — Copenhagen Study Abroad (Design & UX Principles)

sections.headline: Building a mobile guide for Danmarks Tekniske Museum.
sections.body: A museum with over a century of machines and a static desktop website. Visitors on the floor had no guide, no context, no way to find their way around. I designed and built a mobile app from scratch.

items.label: My Role
items.value: Lead UX Designer, research through prototype

items.label: Methods
items.value: Heuristic evaluation, on-site surveys, card sorting, IA design, wireframing

items.label: Deliverable
items.value: Full Figma prototype and handoff spec

sections.label: The problem
sections.headline: A century of machines, and no way to find your way through them.
sections.body: A static desktop website, printed room labels, and whichever staff member happened to be nearby. That was the whole guide. Front-desk staff fielded the same questions on repeat instead of doing the parts of their job that needed a person, and there was no data on what visitors were missing or why.

sections.label: Research
sections.headline: Learning from four museums before building anything.
sections.body: Heuristic evaluation against four comparable apps (MoMA, The Met, Natural History Museum London, Designmuseum Danmark), scored on wayfinding, content depth, discoverability, and family use. Then 12 interviews and 20 on-site surveys to check the gaps I found actually matched what our visitors were struggling with.

items.text: Wayfinding, visitors got lost. None of the 4 apps surfaced real-time floor positioning in an understandable way.
Contextual depth, wall labels weren't enough. Visitors wanted more about the machines they were looking at, in plain language.
Family route planning, no competitor had solved it. Parents with young children had no curated path through the collection.
Discoverability, visitors found exhibitions by accident. No app surfaced upcoming events or highlighted current exhibitions at entry.

sections.text: I wanted to know more about the machines I was looking at, but there was just a small label. I gave up and moved on.

sections.title: Affinity Map, 20 visitor surveys clustered by behaviour and need
sections.sub: In-person surveys at comparable institutions. 4 opportunity clusters emerged from 80+ observation notes.

clusters.label: Wayfinding Problems
notes: "I had no idea where anything was"
Spent 15 mins looking for the computer exhibit
Couldn't tell which floor I was on

clusters.label: Contextual Depth
notes: "I wanted to know how this machine worked, not just when it was made"
Kids asked questions the labels couldn't answer
Didn't realise objects were connected across eras

clusters.label: Family and Route Planning
notes: Young kids got overwhelmed by the full floor
"We gave up after 45 mins because the kids were done"

clusters.label: Event and Booking Discovery
notes: "The website didn't list upcoming events clearly"
Discovered an event only because someone mentioned it
"When does the next demo start? No one could tell me."

sections.label: IA
sections.headline: Card sort to four tabs.
sections.body: Card sort with 48 items and 8 people. Four clusters came out cleanly: Home, History, Events, Map. The decade timeline (1900 through 1970, each era showing one hero machine) came out of the IA work and ended up being the thing that made the app feel different.

sections.title: Early wireframes, week 3
sections.sub: Produced right after the card sort, when the tab structure was confirmed but individual screen interactions were still being worked out.

sections.label: Design
sections.headline: A blueprint, not a brochure.
sections.body: Technical grid lines, monospaced type, cobalt blue on off-white. Everything references the engineering precision of the collection itself. The decade timeline was the signature interaction, prototyped across 3 rounds: tap a decade, one hero object, no scrolling required. I don't start from a mood board, I start from what the thing actually is. A museum of machines should read like engineering, not like every other museum app with a hamburger menu and rounded cards.

sections.label: The four tabs
sections.headline: Home, History, Events, Map. One job each.
sections.body: History: four decade tabs, tap one for a hero machine and a link into the collection. Events: current exhibitions with a one-tap path to booking. Exhibits: era, category, and plain-language description, everything a wall label has no room for. Map: floor plan with exhibit pins, plus a one-tap family route through the collection, something none of the four competitor apps had solved.

items.l: Competitor museum apps evaluated against Nielsen heuristics
User personas mapped and designed against

sections.label: Prototype
sections.headline: Built and deployed
sections.body: Built in HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript on GitHub Pages. Every tab works, every transition is real. I wrote the routing, the decade selector, the event cards, and the map from scratch.

40 screens before I got external feedback on the nav. If I'd done that card sort review at week 3 instead of week 6, I would have caught a nav overlap between History and Exhibits much earlier. The map is also where I'd spend more time: hardest to build, and the thing visitors cared about most.

sections.headline: The decade timeline was the piece that got called out in review.
sections.body: It's not a pattern borrowed from anywhere, it was made for this museum. Every screen was annotated and delivered as a Figma handoff.
